Lawmaking teaching explains which bills originate in the House, Senate amendment power, inquiries, budget limits, and override. Executive teaching describes control, appointments, emergency action, and clemency.

Judicial teaching explains actual disputes, constitutional review in a proper case, and appointment screening. Office comparisons distinguish age, citizenship, residence, experience, profession, and prior candidacy.
Checks and balances are explained through actual veto, override, confirmation, impeachment, and review directions rather than labels alone.
House size includes the unless-law-provides-otherwise qualification; district rules exclude party-list; consecutive terms are not lifetime totals; full membership is distinguished from attendance.

Emergency action requires invasion/rebellion and public safety, has initial time/reporting limits, revocation/review and extension conditions, and does not displace the Constitution or working courts.

Pardon excludes impeachment, follows final judgment, and needs COMELEC advice for election offenses; amnesty needs Congress. Judicial review needs a proper case; appointment consent and natural-born requirements are not applied indiscriminately. Age alone is expressly insufficient.
